My research leverages computational and statistical methods to study organized crime, migration, and violence.

I am an Assistant Professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of California, Davis. I received my Ph.D. in Sociology from the University of California, Los Angeles.

My research examines how criminal networks evolve, how criminal organizations produce and reproduce violence, and the risks migrants face while crossing contested territories. I also use spatial statistical methods to study the geographies of labor migration in the United States.

Research

  • Criminal networks & violence. The structure and evolution of criminal organizations, their alliances and conflicts, and the consequences of state interventions.
  • Migration & contested territories. The relationship between organized crime, territorial contestation, and risks for migrants at the U.S.–Mexico border, alongside the spatial patterns of labor migration.
  • Computational social science. Social network analysis, machine learning, and statistical methods for studying relationships, hidden ties, and spatial processes.
